newsitem.title: USA: FTC chief vows to stop anti-competitive marketing.
newsitem.headline: FTC chief vows to stop anti-competitive marketing.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission Thursday began a crackdown on companies that curb price competition, announcing that an American Home Product division agreed to pay all 50 U.S. states $7.3 million for a rebate scheme.
The money settles charges that American Cyanamid used rebates as a way of inducing dealers to sell its herbicides and pesticides above a set price.

"I don't think it's going to be the last experiment with this kind of mininum resale price maintenance," FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky said in an interview. "We're going to watch carefully to make sure these varieties of resale price maintenance are declared illegal."
The Parsippany, N.J.-based company defended the practice, saying in a statement that its rebate programmes were "pro-competitive and lawful."
American Home Products said it agreed to settle merely to avoid the "burden and expense of litigation."
But only one of the five FTC commissioners agreed with the company, while the other four voted against the practices of American Cyanamid.

It is illegal for companies to get agreements setting minimum prices retailers must charge for their products. To get around that law, many companies have set up inducements for their distributors to maintain minimum prices.
The question is at what point those inducements cross the line of legality.
The answer may be that some already have crossed the line.
"We have some investigations in the pipeline," said Pitofsky. "Maybe not identical conduct, but similar conduct."
Pitofsky said that until now, the FTC has been preoccupied by the huge and growing number of mergers, because "we're in the greatest wave of mergers, I think, this country has ever seen."
But now, he said, that is going to change. Pitofsky said he wants the commission also to focus on other kinds of actions that are raising questions under antitrust laws.
American Cyanamid's problematic conduct began in 1989 and continued for four years in the market for crop protection chemicals, which was worth $1 billion to the company in 1995.
The company offered rebates of up to 12 percent to 2,500 dealers, who followed the prices it set. The FTC said the vast majority of dealers accepted the rebates.

Florida began investigating American Cyanamid in 1994, a spokesman for the country's attorneys general said. When American Home Products acquired American Cyanamid later that year, it dropped the rebate programmes.
